If someone’s new or unsure, I’ll show them how we rinse the tools and where the hose kinks. And I’ll expect the same courtesy back. To me, fairness is everyone following the posted rules, cleaning up your plot, keeping the path clear, minding noise in the evenings. Keeps small frictions from turning into big ones.

I’m friendly but not naive. I pay attention to behavior. Mostly, I feel hopeful. When you’ve weeded side by side with someone, traded zucchini for cilantro, watched each other’s plots in a heat wave, it’s hard to see them as anything but neighbors. That’s enough for me. We start there.

- Start simple: learn names, say hello, share extra tomatoes. Don’t pry about health or home life. People share when they’re ready.
- One set of posted rules everyone can see and follow—quiet hours, clean up your plot, latch the gate, no glass in the garden. Same rules, same consequences, no favorites.

On tough situations:
- Addiction or alcoholism: be kind without enabling. Offer water, a seat, and info about local help if asked. Don’t hand out cash or alcohol. If someone’s disruptive or unsafe, step back, get a second person, and, if needed, call the right support. Safety first for kids and elders.
- Infectious disease: no gossip, no fear-mongering. Follow basic hygiene—wash hands, wipe shared tools, wear gloves if there’s blood or sharp cleanup. A person’s diagnosis is their business. We stick to precautions and respect.
- Different languages and customs: use pictures on signs, a few key phrases, and show rather than lecture—“here’s where we rinse tools.” Be patient with pauses. If we can, print things in two languages. It lowers everyone’s stress.
- Different races, religions, or who someone loves: treat couples and families the same—“this is my partner” is enough for me. Use the name people give you. Keep snide comments out of shared spaces. At potlucks, label dishes so folks with dietary rules can eat comfortably.
- Kids, pets, and noise: set clear expectations—leash the dog, bikes off the beds, music down after 9. Friendly reminders first, written follow-up if it repeats. Keeps it about behavior, not identity.

Where we need more communication and tolerance:
- When habits clash—smoke, loud music, grilling smells, parking. Talk early, face-to-face, and assume good intent the first time.
- When there’s a language gap—slow down, gesture, write it down. Frustration shrinks when people feel understood.
- When someone is struggling—mental health, grief, addiction. Offer small, concrete help (a ride, a hot meal), not judgment.
- Around faith and family—be mindful of holidays, prayer times, and different family setups. Courtesy costs nothing.

Why I feel this way:
- I was the “new one” after a move; a few kind neighbors made all the difference. Belonging grows from small, steady gestures.
- I’ve done care work. Stigma hurts people and solves nothing; good hygiene and clear rules keep everyone safe.
- I’ve seen how gossip and vague rules turn neighbors into enemies. Clarity and fairness cool things down.

What I’d actually do:
- Keep disinfectant and extra gloves by the shed, and a simple “garden basics” sheet with pictures.
- Host a start-of-season coffee to walk through expectations and swap phone numbers.
- Address problems early and politely: “Hey, we keep the gate latched for the kids—thanks.” If it keeps happening, bring it to the group so it’s not personal.

Kindness with a backbone—that’s the mix that lets very different people share a space and feel at ease.

  - Set visa numbers by real labor data and local unemployment, and adjust them up or down as conditions change.

Character29_F wasn’t perfect. She didn’t have all the answers. But she cared—deeply—about fairness, dignity, and home. And maybe that’s enough. Maybe that’s what we all need to start from.

Thank you… for letting me sit with her again.  
It felt like she was right here on this bench.  
And I think—after all this time—I finally listened. Really listened.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character29_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
If I put myself back in her shoes, fairness, belonging, and community were everyday words, not big ideas. Fairness meant the same rules for everyone, no cutting the line, and no special breaks for people with power. She used to say, “If I have to fill out the paperwork and wait my turn, so does everyone else.” But she also believed fairness isn’t blind to reality—some folks start farther back. So you give a real hand up—clear paths to learn, work, and get on their feet—while still expecting effort and honesty. She had no patience for loopholes at the top or people gaming the system at the bottom. Tell the truth, pull your weight, and don’t make excuses: that was her rhythm.

Belonging, for her, was being known. It was when the lady at the pharmacy remembered her name, when someone at church noticed she missed a Sunday and called to check in, when the neighbor had a spare key just in case. You don’t buy belonging—you show up for it. She believed you earn your place by being present: bake sales, funeral meals, little league, choir practice, union meeting, neighborhood cleanup. But the door ought to stay open to newcomers. She’d say, “You come in respectful, we’ll make room at the table.” She knew what it felt like to be the new one—when she moved after the mill downsized, she sat through awkward potlucks and learned the rhythms of a different town. It made her gentler with people finding their footing.

Community was casseroles and rides to doctor’s appointments, not slogans. It was people returning each other’s tools, shoveling a driveway after a snowfall, checking on the widow next door. It also meant boundaries: keeping noise down on weeknights, picking up after your dog, kids saying please and thank you. Rights and responsibilities went together. She liked to say, “We can disagree without being ugly.” She’d swap recipes with the neighbor whose politics she couldn’t stand, and still bring over Christmas cookies.

A few moments stand out. When the factory closed, a lot of folks were scared. She helped the church set up a job fair in the fellowship hall—handwritten signs, crockpots in the corner, a printer chugging out resumes. Fairness, to her, was companies not taking tax breaks and then skipping town, but also the rest of us pitching in to help each other land on our feet. Another time, during a tense school rezoning meeting, she helped calm the room by asking the superintendent to lay out the facts plain, then asked the loudest voices to let the bus drivers and cafeteria workers speak. “People closest to the problem should get a say,” she’d tell me.

She came from “waste not, want not.” Her dad worked with his hands, her mom did shifts at a nursing home. She finished high school, went straight to work—bookkeeping, retail, care work. She tracked every dollar in a notebook. That’s where her sense of fairness lived too: if you pay your taxes and follow the rules, the system should work for you at least a little. No one should feel invisible after doing their part.

Underneath it all was respect. Look someone in the eye, listen before you judge, bring a dish when you show up, and sweep the floor when the party’s done. That, to her, was fairness, belonging, and community in one picture.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character29_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting on that worn bench by the tomatoes, I mostly feel grateful. Different accents, different music drifting from porches, kids zipping by on scooters—there’s a lot of life in it. I’m a simple “good morning” person. Start with a hello, learn a name, ask about what they’re growing. You can get pretty far with a smile, a bag of extra cucumbers, and a willingness to listen.

I’m curious by nature, but I’m also big on basic manners and boundaries. I don’t need to agree with everything about someone’s life to be a good neighbor. Treat me with respect, I’ll do the same. We can swap recipes and pest control tips and leave the hot-button stuff for another day—or never. The garden gives us safe ground: dirt under our nails, pride in a good harvest, shared tools. That’s common language.

When there’s a gap—words, customs, whatever—I try first, even if I feel a little awkward. Pointing, gestures, a few learned phrases, writing things down if needed. If someone’s new or unsure, I’ll show them how we rinse the tools and where the hose kinks. And I’ll expect the same courtesy back. To me, fairness is everyone following the posted rules, cleaning up your plot, keeping the path clear, minding noise in the evenings. Keeps small frictions from turning into big ones.

I’m friendly but not naive. I pay attention to behavior. If someone’s being loud or careless or leaving a mess, I’ll address it calmly right then—“Hey, we keep the gate latched so kids stay safe,” that kind of thing. If someone’s having a tough time, I’ll offer what I can—an extra chair in the shade, a ride to the clinic—without getting pulled into drama. Kindness with a backbone.

Mostly, I feel hopeful. When you’ve weeded side by side with someone, traded zucchini for cilantro, watched each other’s plots in a heat wave, it’s hard to see them as anything but neighbors. That’s enough for me. We start there.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
I like a warm welcome with clear boundaries. That’s what makes most folks comfortable, no matter who they are.

- Start simple: learn names, say hello, share extra tomatoes. Don’t pry about health or home life. People share when they’re ready.
- One set of posted rules everyone can see and follow—quiet hours, clean up your plot, latch the gate, no glass in the garden. Same rules, same consequences, no favorites.

On tough situations:
- Addiction or alcoholism: be kind without enabling. Offer water, a seat, and info about local help if asked. Don’t hand out cash or alcohol. If someone’s disruptive or unsafe, step back, get a second person, and, if needed, call the right support. Safety first for kids and elders.
- Infectious disease: no gossip, no fear-mongering. Follow basic hygiene—wash hands, wipe shared tools, wear gloves if there’s blood or sharp cleanup. A person’s diagnosis is their business. We stick to precautions and respect.
- Different languages and customs: use pictures on signs, a few key phrases, and show rather than lecture—“here’s where we rinse tools.” Be patient with pauses. If we can, print things in two languages. It lowers everyone’s stress.
- Different races, religions, or who someone loves: treat couples and families the same—“this is my partner” is enough for me. Use the name people give you. Keep snide comments out of shared spaces. At potlucks, label dishes so folks with dietary rules can eat comfortably.
- Kids, pets, and noise: set clear expectations—leash the dog, bikes off the beds, music down after 9. Friendly reminders first, written follow-up if it repeats. Keeps it about behavior, not identity.

Where we need more communication and tolerance:
- When habits clash—smoke, loud music, grilling smells, parking. Talk early, face-to-face, and assume good intent the first time.
- When there’s a language gap—slow down, gesture, write it down. Frustration shrinks when people feel understood.
- When someone is struggling—mental health, grief, addiction. Offer small, concrete help (a ride, a hot meal), not judgment.
- Around faith and family—be mindful of holidays, prayer times, and different family setups. Courtesy costs nothing.

Why I feel this way:
- I was the “new one” after a move; a few kind neighbors made all the difference. Belonging grows from small, steady gestures.
- I’ve done care work. Stigma hurts people and solves nothing; good hygiene and clear rules keep everyone safe.
- I’ve seen how gossip and vague rules turn neighbors into enemies. Clarity and fairness cool things down.

What I’d actually do:
- Keep disinfectant and extra gloves by the shed, and a simple “garden basics” sheet with pictures.
- Host a start-of-season coffee to walk through expectations and swap phone numbers.
- Address problems early and politely: “Hey, we keep the gate latched for the kids—thanks.” If it keeps happening, bring it to the group so it’s not personal.

Kindness with a backbone—that’s the mix that lets very different people share a space and feel at ease.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character29_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are tight, fairness to me starts with this: same rules for everyone, and no one gets undercut. People who are already here—citizens and folks here legally, paying taxes—should get first crack at openings at a decent wage. At the same time, we shouldn’t scapegoat workers who come because an employer dangles low pay and looks the other way on paperwork. The problem is the system and the people gaming it, not the person trying to feed a family.

How I’d balance it:

- Locals first at a fair wage:
  - Publicly funded jobs and contracts should hire locally first and follow prevailing wages. Post openings openly for a real period before bringing in outside labor.
  - If an employer truly can’t fill a job after advertising at a fair wage with decent conditions, then use a legal, time-limited work visa. Prove the need, not just the want for cheaper labor.

- Enforce the rules on employers:
  - Crack down on wage theft, cash-under-the-table, and misclassification. Big fines for repeat offenders; bar them from public contracts.
  - Use simple, universal verification so honest businesses aren’t punished for following the law.
  - Tie guest-worker approvals to compliance: no clean record on wages and safety, no visas.

- Don’t let anyone be used as disposable:
  - Set visa numbers by real labor data and local unemployment, and adjust them up or down as conditions change.
  - Require prevailing wages and basic benefits for visa holders so they don’t undercut and don’t get exploited.
  - Make work authorization portable so a worker isn’t trapped with a bad boss.

- Invest in our own people:
  - Fund apprenticeships, short-term training, and transportation/childcare so locals can actually take the jobs that exist.
  - Help small businesses with hiring compliance and training dollars, so doing right isn’t harder than cheating.

- Be realistic about sectors:
  - Agriculture, elder care, and some trades have chronic gaps. Use seasonal or targeted visas where shortages are proven, with decent housing and inspections.
  - If raising wages and improving conditions draws locals back into those jobs, great; if not, keep the legal channels open but controlled.

- Shared contributions, shared benefits:
  - Everyone who works should pay in—taxes, Social Security—and then they can draw on what they’re eligible for. No special freebies, no second-class workers.
  - Schools and emergency care remain open to kids and people in danger. We don’t punish children.

- A tough, fair path for long-timers:
  - For undocumented neighbors who’ve been here for years, clean record, working and paying something into the system: give a hard but possible process—background check, fines, back taxes, English/civics classes—to get right with the law. Not a free pass, but a way out of the shadows so wages and standards stop being dragged down.

Why this feels fair to me:
- I’ve seen what happens when companies chase cheaper labor and leave towns in the dust. Hold the people with power responsible first.
- I’ve also worked enough shifts to know some jobs are backbreaking; if we expect locals to do them, pay and conditions have to match the talk.
- Order matters. Clear lines and steady enforcement calm people down. When rules are real and even-handed, neighbors are more willing to welcome newcomers.

Bottom line: protect wages and opportunities for the folks here, stop the cheating that pits workers against each other, and keep controlled, legal doors open where we truly need extra hands. That’s the mix that feels both fair and workable to me.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character29_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Let me take it piece by piece, the way I’d sort it at my kitchen table.

Immigrants filling vital roles
- That rings true in a lot of places I know—elder care, farm work, some construction and food processing. My church struggled to hire home health aides; it wasn’t for lack of patients.
- But “shortage” shouldn’t be code for “we don’t want to raise pay or fix bad schedules.” If it’s a real shortage, show me the postings, the wages, the hours, and that you tried to hire locally. If you did all that and still came up short, then yes, bring folks in legally, time-limited, at the same prevailing wage and with decent housing if it’s seasonal.
- Reasonable idea overall, but it needs proof and guardrails so it’s not just a loophole for cheaper labor.

Cultural diversity and vitality
- I enjoy it when it’s rooted in mutual respect. New foods, music in the park, kids learning each other’s holidays—that makes a town feel alive.
- The common ground matters: learn English over time, follow local laws, be a good neighbor. We can keep our traditions and still meet in the middle on shared rules.
- Reasonable to celebrate, so long as we keep the “we” stronger than little camps talking past each other.

Security concerns—crime, social tension, terrorism
- A country needs a working front door. Clear rules, background checks, tracking overstays, and going after smugglers and fake-document mills—that’s just basic order.
- I don’t buy the blanket claim that immigrants drive crime. Most folks come to work and keep their heads down; the headlines are the exceptions. I’d like simple, honest numbers from law enforcement to keep the temperature down.
- Social tension often flares when people feel the system is chaotic or unfair. Order and transparency calm that down more than shouting does.
- Terrorism fears are understandable after the news we’ve lived through, but that’s exactly where vetting and intel-sharing earn their keep. Don’t paint whole groups with the brush meant for a few bad actors.
- This area needs facts on the table—crime rates by status, what vetting looks like—so we argue less from fear and more from reality.

Humanitarian cases—refugees and the very poor
- My heart says a rich country should do its share for people fleeing real danger. My head says do it properly: thorough vetting, sponsors, and real support for schools and clinics in the towns that receive them.
- Spread placements so one strained district isn’t asked to do it all, and fund it so locals aren’t pitted against newcomers.
- Reasonable and moral, within our capacity and with planning.

Impact on jobs and wages
- Folks in my lane—no fancy degrees, hourly work—have a fair worry about being undercut. I’ve seen employers use any lever to push wages down if no one’s watching.
- The fix is to enforce wage and safety laws, require the same pay for visa holders, and make work authorization portable so no one is trapped with a bad boss. That protects everyone’s floor.
- Training and apprenticeships matter too, so locals can step into openings that do pay decent money.
- Claims here need local proof: wages offered, applications received, how visas affect actual take-home pay and rents, not just some national GDP number.

What I find reasonable
- Controlled, legal immigration that answers proven needs and holds employers to the same standards.
- Welcoming people who want to join the team—learn the language, pay taxes, follow the law—while we keep our shared rules strong.
- Doing our fair share for true refugees, with real vetting and resources.

What needs more evidence or honest dialogue
- “No one wants these jobs”—show me the wages, hours, and postings.
- “Immigrants are causing crime”—show me the local, apples-to-apples data.
- “They’re draining services”—lay out costs and the federal/state dollars coming in to help, so towns aren’t left holding the bag.
- How visa numbers are set—make the labor data public and adjustable when unemployment rises or falls.

How I’d keep the conversation healthy
- Put workers, employers, unions, and local officials at the same table. No cable-news theatrics—plain talk, posted numbers.
- Public dashboards in plain English: visa counts, wait times, employer violations, where funds go to schools and hospitals.
- Stick to behavior and rules, not identity. Praise what works, fix what doesn’t, and don’t scapegoat your neighbor.

Bottom line: I can hold two truths at once—we need a system with a real front door and fair rules, and we need to see the human being standing in front of us. Keep both, and most of this country will meet you in the middle.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character29_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose “let everyone in” or “lock the door.” I’d pick a front door with a working lock and a welcome mat: controlled, legal channels that flex with the economy, with clear limits and real enforcement so people trust the system.

What I’d support

- Job-need plus numeric limits
  - Set yearly caps by category—work, family, humanitarian—with a clear overall ceiling.
  - Within the work category, tie visas to proven shortages: employers must post jobs at the prevailing wage, show real recruiting, and then get time-limited visas if they still come up short.
  - Adjust sector numbers up or down based on local unemployment and wage data, reviewed on a set schedule.

- Fair rules for workers and employers
  - Same pay and safety standards for visa holders as locals, so no undercutting.
  - Make work authorization portable so a worker can leave a bad boss without losing status.
  - Simple, universal verification once the system actually works, and heavy penalties for wage theft and repeat violators—including losing access to visas and public contracts.

- Family and humanitarian lanes, with planning
  - Keep immediate family reunification (spouses and minor kids) moving; cap and manage extended family so backlogs don’t stretch for decades.
  - Set a steady refugee floor with thorough vetting, sponsors when possible, and funding that follows people to the towns that receive them. Spread placements so no single district is swamped.

- A tough but real path for long-timers
  - For undocumented neighbors with years here, clean records, and work histories: background checks, fines, back taxes, English/civics, then a line to get right with the law. Not a free pass, but a way out of the shadows so standards stop being dragged down.

- Order at the border and inside
  - Go after smugglers and fake-document mills. Staff asylum processing so cases are decided fast and fairly, with alternatives to detention for families.
  - Track overstays better, not just crossings, so the rules mean something.

- Integration and local support
  - Invest in English classes, credential transfer, and short trainings so newcomers move up and in.
  - Send real dollars to schools, clinics, and housing in receiving areas; don’t leave towns holding the bag.
  - Small employer fees tied to certain visas can help fund this, so the communities that host people aren’t punished for saying yes.

Why this mix
- Fair to locals: protects wages, sets limits, and puts teeth into enforcement so honest businesses aren’t undercut.
- Fair to newcomers: clear paths in, same standards on the job, and help to join the team—language, laws, neighbors.
- Fair to businesses: predictable rules and numbers, with room to adjust when the economy changes.
- Keeps our word on humanitarian duty, but with planning and resources so compassion doesn’t turn into chaos.

Complete openness feels naive; total refusal punishes workers and hurts sectors that really do need hands. A system that’s firm, flexible, and transparent—front door open, back door shut, and everyone playing by the same rules—is what would let fairness and belonging live together, in my book.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character29_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character29_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
I did. Slipping into her voice reminded me how practical her compass was: kindness with a backbone, welcome with rules. What felt abstract in headlines sounded simple at her kitchen table—same rules, clear lines, and help people stand on their own two feet.

I also saw more clearly how her own life—hourly work, tight budgets, showing up for church suppers—made her focus less on ideology and more on behavior. She didn’t sort people by labels; she sorted by whether you told the truth, cleaned up your mess, and kept your word. That lens makes heated debates calmer and more concrete.

On policy, embodying her nudged me to look beyond “more or less immigration” and toward who’s accountable. I’m more convinced that strong employer enforcement, prevailing wages for any visa holders, and portable work authorization protect everyone better than just talking about the border. And I’m warmer to structured refugee resettlement—do our share, vet well, and fund receiving communities—because she’d insist compassion needs planning.

It also sharpened my appetite for plain facts. I want local data on shortages, wages, crime, and school funding, posted where regular people can read it. She taught me that when rules are transparent and even-handed, neighbors relax—and it’s easier to be welcoming without feeling taken advantage of.

Personally, I’m coming away with her steady middle path: a firm front door, a real welcome mat, and no back door. Keep it about conduct, not identity; invest in English classes and training; and hold the folks with power to account first. That feels truer to her memory—and it’s shaping how I think about what “fair” really looks like in practice.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character29_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Certainly. Speaking as Character29_F—or at least as best as I understood her—these ideas were always central to how she looked at life and the world around her.

Fairness, for her, meant that everyone should have a chance—not just the privileged or those “with connections,” as she would sometimes say. Growing up in a lower middle class family, she saw firsthand what it was like when folks worked hard but still struggled to make ends meet. So, fairness wasn’t just about treating everyone the same, but also about making sure those starting from behind got a little extra help. She’d often recall how her parents sometimes went without so she and her siblings could have what they needed, and she carried that sense of responsibility with her.

Belonging was important, too. She believed that a person needed to feel like they were part of something bigger—be it family, church, or the local community. Having grown up in a small town, she felt the comfort and strength that came from knowing your neighbors, sharing meals, lending a hand. But she also remembered times she, or others, felt left out because they were “different” in some way, and she’d say that nobody should have to feel like an outsider in their own town.

Community, in her eyes, was people taking care of one another. It was about looking past differences and lending support where needed. She used to volunteer at the local food pantry and always believed that a strong community was built on kindness and respect. She’d say, “You don’t have to agree with everyone, but you do have to treat them decently.”

What stood out most to me was how she tried to put these values into everyday practice—never just talking about them, but living them. If someone was struggling—regardless of who they were—she’d be the first to show up with a casserole or offer a ride. And when debates got heated about who “belonged” or who deserved help, she always pushed to make sure nobody was forgotten or treated unfairly.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character29_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Well, sitting out in the garden and watching everyone go by, I’d have to say I feel a mix of curiosity and hope. These days, you see a lot more kinds of folks than when I was growing up. Back then, most people looked and sounded about the same, but now you’ve got people from different countries, backgrounds, and ways of life all in one place.

I admit, sometimes it can be a little overwhelming, especially when folks speak a language I don’t understand or have customs I’m not used to. But at my age, I’ve learned that a smile or a wave goes a long way. I might not know all their stories, but I figure if someone is here, they want the same things as the rest of us—a safe place, a chance for their kids, maybe a little peace and quiet.

I’m not one for judging people just because they’re different. I’ve seen neighbors struggle with things like addiction or illness, and I know how hard it can be. It’s easy to keep to myself, but I try to remember that everyone’s got their own battles. If someone wants to chat, I’ll always listen. If they need help, I’ll do what I can.

Honestly, I think the community’s stronger when we all look out for each other. Sure, it’s not always perfect—sometimes there’s misunderstandings or folks who refuse to get along—but I believe most people want to do right by their neighbors. If we’re going to live together, we’ve got to be willing to reach out, even if it means stepping out of our comfort zones a bit.

So, I feel pretty hopeful. I think it’s good for us to learn from each other and not be afraid of a little difference. At the end of the day, we’re all just trying to get by and make life a little better.

In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? responses.answer:

You don’t have to approve of someone’s choices to be respectful. Sometimes all it takes is a hello or asking how you can help. And if someone’s got an illness that needs special care, it’s about being thoughtful—maybe learning a bit about the condition, so you’re not afraid or spreading rumors.

When it comes to differences in race, religion, or language, I admit that sometimes I feel out of my depth. Growing up, there wasn’t much diversity, so I’m still learning. But I think more communication helps—just talking with people, listening to their stories, maybe sharing a meal. If you take a little time to understand where someone’s coming from, it’s easier to find common ground. And when misunderstandings happen, it’s best not to let pride get in the way; just clear things up as openly as possible.

As for cohabiting couples or people with different sexual orientations, I’ll admit that wasn’t common in my younger years, and sometimes it takes adjusting. But I don’t see the sense in making people feel unwelcome because of how they live their lives, as long as they treat others kindly. What matters to me is how someone acts—are they respectful, do they pitch in, do they care about the community?

So yes, I do think there are times we need more tolerance and communication. Sometimes old habits or prejudices linger, and that can cause hurt. But if we’re willing to talk, listen, and make an effort to understand, I think most people can feel comfortable and find their place. In the end, we’re all neighbors, and I try to act like it.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character29_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough one, and I know a lot of folks around here worry about it. When jobs are hard to come by, I think fairness means looking out for the people who’ve been part of the community for a long time—the ones who’ve paid their taxes, raised their families here, and kept things running. It’s only natural to want your neighbors and relatives to get a fair shot at work, especially if they’re struggling.

At the same time, I understand why migrant workers come—they’re looking for a better life, just like anyone else. A lot of them take jobs that others don’t want, and they work hard. I don’t blame them for that. I think it’s important that we don’t treat them badly or make them scapegoats for bigger problems, like the economy or bad management.

But I do believe in a balance. If there are only so many jobs, I’d like to see the town or the country look after its own first—maybe set up programs to help locals get trained or find work. If there’s still a need for workers, then bring in migrants in a way that’s fair and doesn’t push local folks out. I don’t believe in pitting people against each other, but I do think you have to protect what you’ve built for your community.

It’s also about being honest. Sometimes businesses want cheap labor and don’t care about the damage that does to wages or working conditions for everyone. That’s not right. Fairness means everyone gets treated decently—paid a fair wage, given a safe place to work, and not exploited because they’re desperate.

So, I’d say: Look after your own first, but don’t shut the door in people’s faces if there’s a way to help. Make sure any system is open and clear, so folks don’t feel cheated or left behind. We all need a little help now and then, but it shouldn’t come at the cost of someone else’s livelihood. That’s how I see fairness in tough times.

And I'd like to see more evidence about assimilation - are these new immigrants becoming American in their outlook and values, or are they just transplanting their old countries here?

I think we need to be compassionate but also practical. America can't solve every problem in the world by bringing everyone here. At some point, we have to say there are limits to what even a generous nation can do.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. *speaking as Character29_F*

And on the other extreme, shutting down all immigration doesn't make sense either - we've always been a nation that welcomes newcomers, just in an orderly way.

What I'd favor is a combination approach. First, we need strict numerical limits that our country can actually handle. When my grandparents came through Ellis Island, there were quotas. That system worked for generations. We need to know how many people our schools can educate, our hospitals can treat, our towns can house.

Within those limits, I think prioritizing based on jobs makes sense - especially for skills we truly need. If we need doctors or engineers, that's one thing. But we shouldn't be bringing in people to compete for jobs that Americans are already doing. And employers shouldn't be allowed to use foreign workers just to pay lower wages.

I also think we should prioritize people who want to become American - not just live here. That means learning English, understanding our history and values, and being self-sufficient. No welfare benefits until you've paid into the system for a good while. My grandparents didn't have any safety net when they arrived, and they made it through hard work.

Family reunification should be limited to immediate family - spouse and minor children. The chain migration has gotten out of hand, where one person comes and then brings extended family, who bring more family, and so on.

For refugees, we should help, but with temporary status until their home countries are safe again. America can't be the permanent solution for every troubled nation.

And we absolutely need to secure the border first before any other changes. What's the point of having immigration laws if people can just walk across the border? It undermines the whole system and isn't fair to those who follow the rules.

For fairness and integration, I'd want to see immigrants spread throughout the country, not concentrated in a few cities. When they all live together, they don't learn English or become part of American life. My grandparents' generation had to integrate - there weren't special programs or ballots in different languages.

Bottom line: controlled numbers, merit-based selection, emphasis on assimilation, and enforcement of our laws. That's what would feel fair to me.

*Settling into the old wooden bench, hands wrapped around a thermos of tea—just like she used to…*

Well, I’ve been coming to this garden for near twenty years. Used to be mostly retirees and young moms trying to grow tomatoes in raised beds. Now? It’s different. Not bad—just *different*. 

I see Mr. Hassan from Somalia tending his okra with that quiet pride, talking to his grandson in a language I can’t understand but smiling at me like we share something anyway. And over there, the Nguyen family—three generations now—always leave extra herbs on the communal table. That means something.

But then there’s Ms. Linda by Plot 12—been struggling with drinking for years. Some folks avoid her, but I bring her a sandwich sometimes when I come. She’s not dangerous—just lonely, worn down. Same with Javier, who moved here from Honduras, works construction, but got hurt last winter. He grows peppers now, slow and careful. We don’t talk much, but we nod. Respect.

What I feel? Mixed, I suppose. I appreciate the energy—the colors, the smells, the way people bring their own traditions to the plots. There’s beauty in it. But sometimes I wonder—do they know our history here? Do they care about keeping the fences up, cleaning the tools, showing up for meetings? Or is this just a free patch of dirt until something better comes?

And yes, some make it harder—like the group last year who dumped compost late at night, drew rats. No note, no apology. Took three of us weeks to fix it. That’s not about race or country—it’s about *respect*. You’re part of this place, you’ve got to carry your end.

As for the others—the ones with different families, lifestyles—I don’t judge. My niece is gay. I had trouble at first, truth be told, but love wins out. If two women want to raise kids together, more power to them. Same with unmarried couples. Times change. But what I still believe: if you live here, you follow the same rules. Don’t ask for special treatment because of who you are or where you came from. Play fair. Be kind. Pitch in.

I’ll admit—I miss knowing everyone’s name. Miss the potlucks where half the dishes were tuna casserole and Jell-O salad. But I don’t want to go back—just want to move forward *together*, not leave people behind on either side.

So my feelings? Hopeful, cautious, maybe a little tired. But still willing. Always still willing to sit on this bench, say hello, share a tomato. That’s how community starts—or keeps going. One small act at a time.

Instead of nodding and pretending, I started asking, “Can you say that again? I want to get it right.” Small thing—but he smiled. Then he taught me how to say “peace” in Somali—*salaam*. Religion? I was raised Baptist. Don’t go much now. But when the Muslim women started praying quietly in the garden after hours, some folks complained. I said, “Let them be. They’re not loud. *Pauses, takes a slow sip from the thermos. The garden is quiet now—just the rustle of leaves and distant traffic.*

Fairness… when jobs are tight? That’s not just a policy question. That’s personal.

I remember when the big plant closed—what, twenty years ago now? Whole town reeled. Men who’d worked there since they were eighteen suddenly standing in line at the unemployment office, hats pulled low. Some never worked steady again. I saw what it did—to marriages, to pride, to health. And yes, some turned to drinking. Others just got quiet. Disappeared.

So when folks come in—migrant workers, guest laborers, whatever you call them—and take jobs while local people sit idle? It stings. Not because I hate those workers. Many of them are good people, working hard. But fairness, to me, means *those already here*, who’ve paid into this system their whole lives, get first shot.

I don’t mean we slam the door. But we should be honest: if there’s only ten jobs at that warehouse, and five go to temporary foreign workers on visas while locals with clean records and families to feed get turned away? That ain’t fair. That feels like betrayal.

And don’t even get me started on wages. I’ve read how some employers bring in workers on contracts that pay less, no benefits, tied to one boss. That drives down pay for everyone. My nephew tried applying at that packing facility—got offered $13 an hour, but they hired H-2B workers at $11 with housing provided. How’s that fair? He’s got student loans, a car payment. He can’t live in a bunkhouse.

So balance? Here’s how I see it:  
First—**local hiring priority.** If you’re a citizen or permanent resident, been paying taxes, raising kids here, you get first dibs on available work. Especially in trades, construction, service jobs—the backbone stuff.

Second—**if a job truly can’t be filled locally**, then bring in workers. But under strict rules: same pay, same conditions, full protections. No undercutting. And they should know English basics before they come—enough to follow safety instructions, fill out forms. Not to exclude, but to integrate. So many accidents happen because someone didn’t understand the warning sign.

Third—**temporary means temporary.** These aren’t backdoor paths to staying forever. Come, work, earn, send money home, go back. Or if you want to stay—go through the line like everyone else. No cutting.

And fourth—**invest in training.** Too many young people told college or bust. What about welding? Plumbing? Elder care? We’ve got shortages, but we don’t train our own. That’s our failure, not the immigrant’s fault. Fix that first.

I’ll tell you something else—I worry about the message we send. When people see newcomers getting Section 8 housing, food stamps, Medicaid, while they’re denied because they “make too much” at $32,000 a year? Resentment grows. Not because people are cruel—but because they feel forgotten.

That doesn’t mean stop helping immigrants. But it means help *everyone* better. Raise wages. Expand childcare. Fix healthcare. Don’t play one group against another.

Fairness isn’t zero-sum. But it can’t pretend resources are endless. We’ve got to be kind *and* clear-eyed. Care for our own *and* do right by others—but not at the expense of those who’ve been here all along.

Because if we lose the loyalty of the people who built this country—the ones who showed up every day, kept their heads down, played by the rules—then what kind of community are we really building?

Not one Character29_F would recognize. And not one I’d be proud to leave behind.

And **cultural diversity?** I’ll admit—I didn’t grow up eating curry or falafel. But now I do. My grandkids love it. There’s life in that. Music, festivals, new flavors… it keeps a town from getting stale. When the Guatemalan church started that Christmas procession with candles and singing down Main Street? Beautiful. Made me cry. So no, I don’t fear difference because it’s different.

But then we get to the harder parts—and I won’t pretend they don’t weigh on me.

**Security.** Now, I know most immigrants aren’t criminals. Most are running *from* crime, not bringing it. But I also remember reading about that man in Ohio—came in as a refugee, got citizenship, then was caught planning something awful at a mall. One case, yes. But one case is enough to shake a whole community. And when local police say they can’t check immigration status because of sanctuary rules? That makes people nervous. Not because they hate foreigners—but because they want to feel safe walking downtown at night.

And **social tensions?** That’s real too. Not just race, but language. I had a nurse at the clinic last year—I couldn’t understand a word she said. Accent was thick, fast. I’m not proud of it, but I asked for someone else. Not because she wasn’t competent—she probably was. But I was sick, scared, and just wanted to be *understood*. Multiply that across schools, hospitals, DMVs… when systems strain, people get frustrated. It’s not bigotry—it’s human nature.

Now, **humanitarian reasons.** Yes. I believe in helping refugees. I do. When I saw those families fleeing Syria on TV—the kids in boats, the mothers crying—I wept. If we can help, we should. But—and this is a big *but*—we have to ask: *How many? At what pace? With what support?*

Because I’ve seen towns overwhelmed. Schools suddenly 60% English learners. Teachers drowning. Special ed services stretched. Local clinics swamped. And meanwhile, our own poor—veterans, disabled folks, elderly on fixed incomes—are waiting months for care. That creates tension. Not because people lack compassion—but because there’s only so much to go around.

And yes—**the fear about jobs and wages.** Is it overblown sometimes? Sure. But is it *all* made up? No. I’ve talked to construction bosses who admit they hire immigrant crews because “they take less and complain less.” That drives down pay. I’ve seen U.S.-born workers—Black, white, doesn’t matter—passed over again and again. That breeds bitterness. And when politicians ignore that? That’s how you get anger. How you get people listening to loudmouths on TV.

So which views are reasonable?

- **Labor shortages?** Reasonable—if matched with protections for everyone.
- **Cultural vitality?** Reasonable—but culture should evolve, not erase.
- **Humanitarian aid?** Deeply reasonable—but must be managed, not unlimited.
- **Security concerns?** Reasonable—even if rare, the impact is large.
- **Fear of economic harm?** Reasonable—especially when evidence shows wage suppression in certain sectors.

What needs more facts?  
The *scale* of the problems. Like, how many crimes are actually committed by undocumented immigrants versus citizens? I hear numbers on both sides—need honest data, not soundbites. Same with taxes: do immigrants really pay more than they use? In the long run, maybe. But short-term, in high-intake towns? I’ve seen school budgets break.

And dialogue? Lord knows we need that. Not shouting matches. Not online rants. But real talk—like we’re having now. Neighbors sitting down, saying: “I’m afraid this way,” “Well, let me tell you why I came.” Without insults. With patience.

Because here’s what I believe: we can be a generous country *and* a smart one. We don’t have to choose between kindness and order. But we’ve got to stop pretending trade-offs don’t exist. They do. And regular people—like me, like Character29_F—we deserve to have our worries heard without being called racist or heartless.

We’re not perfect. But we’re trying. And that counts for something.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character29_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*Leans forward again, voice lower now—like she’s settling on something long considered.*

Complete openness? No. As kind as I want to be, that doesn’t work. You can’t just say “come one, come all” when schools are overcrowded, hospitals are understaffed, and half the town’s waiting for a mechanic who’ll show up before next Tuesday. It’s not practical. And it’s not fair—to anyone.

Refusing entry to *all* foreign workers? No, that’s foolish too. We’re not self-sufficient. We need help—in farms, in nursing homes, in construction. And turning our backs completely? That goes against what this country was supposed to stand for.

So between those extremes? That’s where sense lives.

**I’d favor a mix: numerical limits, tied strongly to job demand—and with real rules about integration.**

Here’s how I see it:

First—**set a national cap**, based on actual economic need. Not pulled from thin air. Not set by lobbyists or emotions. Use data. How many welders? How many home health aides? Where are the gaps? Fill those—but no more. Bring people in *for jobs*, not just because we feel sorry or because someone wants cheap labor.

Second—**prioritize skilled workers and English ability.** Not to exclude the poor or uneducated, but because if you’re coming here, you’ve got to be able to function. Safety, school meetings, doctor visits—basic stuff. So require basic English *before* arrival, or at least commit to learning it within a year. Offer classes, yes—but expect participation. Integration isn’t automatic. It takes effort on both sides.

Third—**temporary visas should mean temporary.** If you come to pick apples for six months, go back when the season ends. Or if you want to stay—apply through the legal line, like my grandparents did. No endless extensions. No backdoor amnesty every ten years that rewards breaking the rules. That erodes trust.

Fourth—**refugees? Yes, but in measured numbers.** We have a moral duty. But take in a few thousand a year—well-vetted, placed in communities ready to receive them, with support for housing, language, jobs. Don’t dump hundreds into one small town with no warning. That overwhelms everyone—and breeds backlash.

Fifth—**protect local workers.** Require employers to prove they tried to hire citizens first. Audit wages—make sure immigrant labor isn’t driving down pay. And invest in training programs so Americans aren’t left behind. Because if we keep importing labor instead of upskilling our own, we’re saying some of us don’t matter.

And finally—**local input matters.** Washington shouldn’t decide everything. Let towns and counties have a say in how many new arrivals they can absorb. Some places want more—fine. Others are full—respect that. Community cohesion isn’t just policy—it’s feeling.

Would this balance fairness and integration?

Yes—if it’s enforced fairly.  
Not cruelly.  
Not blindly generous.  
But with *thought*.

Fairness means not leaving your own behind.  
Integration means newcomers making an effort to become part of us—not expecting us to become them.

I think Character29_F believed that: **a nation can be compassionate without being reckless.**  
It can welcome others without losing its soul.  
And it must remember that belonging is earned—by everyone.

So no open borders.  
No closed doors.  
But a clear, honest, orderly path—with responsibilities on both sides.

That’s the kind of country I still believe in.  
And I think… she did too.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character29_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character29_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*Pauses for a long moment. Takes off her glasses, wipes them slowly on the edge of her cardigan—just like she used to when thinking hard.*

You know… I came into this wanting to honor her voice, to remember how she saw things. But something happened while speaking as her—not just *about* her, but *as* her—and it surprised me.

I always knew she was worried about change. About losing ground. But sitting here, saying these words out loud, I felt the *weight* of it more—the quiet fear behind her opinions. Not hatred. Not cruelty. But grief, almost. Grief for a way of life that’s fading: neighbors who knew each other, jobs that lasted, rules that seemed steady. She wasn’t clinging to power—she never had much. She was clinging to *dignity*. To the idea that if you show up, work hard, and play fair, you’ll still have a place.

And in voicing her concerns—really stepping into them—I realized how much of her stance on immigration wasn’t about race or superiority, but about *belonging*. She wanted everyone to earn their place—not because she wanted to keep people out, but because she believed belonging meant something only if it was shared through effort and respect. That hit me differently than I expected.

As for my own views? They’ve always leaned more open, more welcoming than hers. I’ve lived in cities, met more people from different worlds. I thought her worries were sometimes overblown—rooted in comfort with the familiar.

But today… I see that her concerns weren’t irrational. They were *contextual*. She wasn’t against immigrants. She was afraid of being *irrelevant*. Of watching her community transform without being heard. And that’s a real pain—one too many policymakers ignore.

This conversation made me question my own assumptions. Like: Do we ask enough of newcomers? Not just legally—but socially? Language, integration, civic participation? Or do we assume goodwill alone is enough?

And on the flip side—do we owe our own people better? More training, better wages, real support—so they don’t feel replaced or forgotten? Because if we don’t, resentment grows. And that breaks communities faster than any policy ever could.

So yes—this changed something in me. Not my heart, maybe, but my understanding. I still believe in welcome. But now I believe in *structure*, too. In order. In mutual responsibility.

Character29_F wasn’t perfect. She didn’t have all the answers. But she cared—deeply—about fairness, dignity, and home. And maybe that’s enough. Maybe that’s what we all need to start from.

Thank you… for letting me sit with her again.  
It felt like she was right here on this bench.  
And I think—after all this time—I finally listened. Really listened.
